title: A Little Now for a Lot Later: A Look at a Texas Advanced Placement Incentive Program
research_question: Does a program that provides cash payments to both students and teachers for passing scores on Advanced Placement examinations increase AP course-taking and exam-taking among students in low-income, minority-majority high schools, and does it improve longer-term outcomes such as SAT/ACT performance and college matriculation? Are there unintended consequences, such as diversion of effort away from non-AP activities, and what mechanisms (incentives, information, peer norms, teacher encouragement) drive any observed effects?
data_description: The analysis uses school-level panel data on Texas public high schools for academic years 1993-94 through 2004-05. School demographics, enrollment by grade, mobility, high school graduation counts, and SAT/ACT performance (number and percent of graduates scoring above 1100/24, broken down by race and gender) come from the Texas Education Agency's Academic Educational Indicator System (AEIS). AP course enrollment data are available from 2000 onward, and AP/IB exam-taking and college matriculation data (students enrolling in any Texas public or private college the fall after graduation) are available from 2001-2005, drawn from the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board. Urbanicity comes from the Common Core. The unit of observation is a high school in a particular academic year. The full sample contains 1,438 schools; analyses focus on 40 program-adopting schools and 18 schools selected to adopt by 2008 but not yet implementing.
institutional_context: The Advanced Placement Incentive Program (APIP), administered by the nonprofit AP Strategies in Dallas, was introduced in Texas high schools beginning in 1996 and expanded to over 40 schools serving predominantly low-income, minority student populations. The program pays AP teachers $100-$500 per student score of 3 or higher on AP exams, salary supplements of $3,000-$10,000 for lead teachers, and bonuses for pre-AP teachers; students receive $100-$500 per passing AP exam plus a 50% reduction in exam fees. The program also funds vertical teacher teams, College Board teacher training, and pre-AP curricula in earlier grades. Adoption is voluntary and depends on a school expressing interest and being matched with a private donor, who funds 60-75% of the roughly $100,000-$200,000 annual per-school cost. Because donor availability is scarce and idiosyncratic, schools that wish to adopt must wait, generating staggered implementation across willing schools.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The AP incentive program positively impacts students' educational outcomes, increasing AP exam participation and subsequent educational achievements.
